\chapter{Hablaba and Hablo --- Two Ways of Looking}
\label{ch:aspect-not-time}
\hlchaptermodality{94}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that the two past tenses differ in viewpoint rather than in time.}

Complete ES-C48-dos-miradas: say whether the two pasts differ in when, and identify which one views an event from outside.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hablaba / habló]{hablaba and habló — two ways of looking}

\label{lesson:ES-C48-dos-miradas}



\begin{quote}
You hold two past tenses. Say \textquotedblleft{}I spoke\textquotedblright{} in both. (\emph{Hablé}. \emph{Hablaba}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: not two times — two viewpoints}]
The obvious guess is that one is further back than the other. It is not. Both describe the same afternoon.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Ayer \textbf{hablé} con Ana.} — Yesterday I spoke with Ana. \emph{Ayer \textbf{hablaba} con Ana.} — Yesterday I was speaking with Ana.
\end{quote}

Same day, same conversation, same two people. What changes is \textbf{where you are standing}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{\textbf{Hablé}} looks at the conversation from outside, finished, as one thing with edges. It happened, it is over, next.
  \item \emph{\textbf{Hablaba}} puts you inside it, while it is still going on. No edges. It is the scenery, not the event.
\end{itemize}

This is why the choice cannot be made by a rule about time. It is made by what you are doing with the sentence: \textbf{reporting something that happened}, or \textbf{setting a scene where something else can happen}.

Grammar books call this \emph{aspect}. The word is not important. The habit is: when you reach for a past tense, you are being asked a question about your own point of view, and you answer it every time whether you notice or not.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
English asks you the same question and lets you dodge it.

\begin{quote}
I spoke. I was speaking. I used to speak.
\end{quote}

Those are three different viewpoints, and English marks them with extra words rather than with the verb itself. Because they are optional, you can say \textquotedblleft{}I spoke\textquotedblright{} for almost anything and be understood.

Spanish put the choice \textbf{inside the verb}, so it is not optional. Every past sentence commits to a viewpoint before it commits to anything else. That is why this is the piece of Spanish that stays difficult longest for English speakers: not because it is complicated, but because it asks a question your first language let you leave unanswered.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hablé\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}hablaba\textquotedblright{} — outside, then inside
  \item \textquotedblleft{}estudié\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}estudiaba\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Do the two pasts differ in \textbf{when}? (\textbf{No} — in how you look at it.) Which one has edges? (The \textbf{preterite}.) Next: the word that lets both of them stand in one sentence.
\end{tcolorbox}
